nodes.question: What socio-economic aspects of nuclear energy are discussed in the collection?
nodes.answer: Perspectives on market readiness, legal frameworks, and international cooperation in nuclear energy are discussed.

nodes.answer: New nuclear reactor concepts must be approved for licensing by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

INTRODUCTION As international industrialization and worldwide population growth continue to occur, future energydemands are projected to increase by approximately 30% by the year 2050. 1According to the Interna- tional Energy Agency S World Energy Outlook2023,2the development and implementation of affordable, clean energy options is imperative to reaching the 1.5 /C176C limit on global warming by 2050 as established by the Paris Agreement.3Fortu- nately, nuclear energy is an attractive sector of the world S future energy portfolio as it is a power-dense energy source capable of producing energy at largescale while being carbon-free and virtually emis- sion-free.4Nuclear energy S ability to provide a consistent, continuous baseload energy with sched-uled downtime occurring only every /C2418 24 months (or longer, depending on reactor type) for refueling makes it a more competitive optionthan some other green energy sources. nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What action did OECD countries take regarding export finance for coal-fired power projects in 2015?
nodes.answer: OECD countries agreed to restrict export finance for coal-fired power projects in 2015.
nodes.paragraph: For example, in 2015 OECD countries agreed to restrict export finance for coal-fired power projects (Liao 2021 ). In 2021 European countries launched the Export Finance for Future (E3F) coalition to specifically align export finance with international climate objectives (E3F 2023 ). In the same year, 34 countries signed the Glasgow Statement, which commits signatories to ending public financial support for international fossil fuel projects (DuFour et al. 2022 ). At the national level, many G20 governments have responded by implementing new climate targets. For example, in 2022 European ECAs committed to ending export credit for fossil fuel energy projects (IISD 2022 ), and several other ECAs, including the Export-Import Bank of the US (Exlm) and the UK Export Finance (UKEF) have announced policies to limit public finance for fossil fuels (DuFour et al. 2022 ). While the pressure on ECAs is likely to increase, we do not have a good understanding of the potential for these public bilateral financial institutions to accelerate a clean energy transition. To the extent that ECAs have been studied, the initial focus has been on tracking financial flows from specific countries, such as China, or focussing on particular fuels, such as coal (Chen et al.

nodes.question: What factors affect the capacity of Export Credit Agencies (ECAs) to support renewable energy industries?
nodes.answer: The capacity of ECAs to respond to demand for export credit from renewable energy industries is contingent on having policy tools that support renewables firms, which may have different needs than firms in oil, gas, and coal industries.
nodes.paragraph: In other words, the effect of a strong domestic green industrial base on levels of export finance for renewables should be positive. This relationship is likely to be stronger when renewable industries are comprised of multinational corporations (MNCs) that are export-orientated with the expertise to seek out export finance. Third is policy tools available to ECAs to accelerate renewable energy and related tech - nologies. The capacity of ECAs to respond to demand for export credit from renewable energy industries is contingent on whether ECAs have the policy tools to support renew - ables firms, whose needs may be different than firms in the oil, gas, and coal industries. For example, in the US and UK domestic content requirements, investment support, and risk aversion, have all affected the extent to which Exlm and UKEF have supported renewable industries. While we contend that these factors are likely to be the most important deter - minants of ECA energy lending cross-nationally, these will vary across political-economic contexts. The next section locates ECAs in the literature on climate finance and energy transitions and presents descriptive data on the energy lending of G20 ECAs.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Ocean thermal energy|Otec policy and regulatory considerations_qna_007
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What factors shape the capacity of Exlm and UKEF to promote renewable energy exports?
nodes.answer: The extent of political control over the bureaucracy, the size and composition of green industrial bases, and the policy tools available to both ECAs.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Achieving a clean energy transition requires global financial flows to be redirected away from fossil fuels and into renewable energy. While capital market actors and multilateral financial institutions have been the subject of significant scholarly attention, public bilat - eral financial institutions, especially Export Credit Agencies (ECAs), have been largely overlooked. This is an important oversight given ECAs are the source of billions of dollars of public finance for fossil fuels, which has helped to lock-in recipient countries to fossil fuel energy systems. Using a panel dataset of ECA transactions in the energy sector, we show that despite some improvements in financial flows after the Paris Agreement in 2015, fossil fuel investments remain pervasive and growth in clean energy investments is mini - mal. To better understand changes in ECA portfolios, we examine the cases of the Export- Import Bank of the United States (Exlm) and UK Export Finance (UKEF). Drawing on elite interviews, we identify three factors that are shaping Exlm S and UKEF S capacity to promote renewable energy exports: the extent of political control over the bureaucracy, the size and composition of green industrial bases, and the policy tools available to both ECAs to support the renewables sector.
